---
title: "The Memory Wall"
subtitle: "Why 3.2× more FLOPS gives only 1.6× speedup, and how to know in advance."
description: "Compare A100 and H100 GPUs to discover that for memory-bound workloads, bandwidth, not compute, determines performance. The most important fallacy in ML systems."
categories: ["node", "beginner"]
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import mlsysim  # installed via `pip install mlsysim` (see workflow)
Engine = mlsysim.Engine

a100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
h100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100
v100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.V100
model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B

flops_v = v100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
flops_a = a100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
flops_h = h100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
bw_v = v100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
bw_a = a100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
bw_h = h100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude

flops_ratio = flops_h / flops_a
bw_ratio = bw_h / bw_a
ridge_v = (v100.compute.peak_flops / v100.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude
ridge_a = (a100.compute.peak_flops / a100.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude
ridge_h = (h100.compute.peak_flops / h100.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude

prof_v100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=v100, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")
prof_a100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=a100, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")
prof_h100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=h100, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")

lat_v = prof_v100.latency.to("ms").magnitude
lat_a = prof_a100.latency.to("ms").magnitude
lat_h = prof_h100.latency.to("ms").magnitude
speedup = lat_a / lat_h

params_b = model.parameters.to("dimensionless").magnitude / 1e9
weights_gb = model.size_in_bytes("fp16").to("GB").magnitude
min_lat_a = (model.size_in_bytes("fp16") / a100.memory.bandwidth).to("ms").magnitude
min_lat_h = (model.size_in_bytes("fp16") / h100.memory.bandwidth).to("ms").magnitude
min_speedup = min_lat_a / min_lat_h

_p_a256 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=a100, batch_size=256, precision="fp16")
_p_h256 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=h100, batch_size=256, precision="fp16")
_sp_256 = (_p_a256.latency / _p_h256.latency).to("dimensionless").magnitude
```

## The Question

NVIDIA's H100 has **`{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`× more FLOP/s** than the A100. **Does upgrading deliver a `{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`×
speedup?**

It does not. For the workloads that matter most in production (LLM inference, recommendation
models, any memory-bound task), the speedup is closer to **`{python} f"{speedup:.1f}"`×** (tracking the **`{python} f"{bw_ratio:.1f}"`×** HBM bandwidth ratio). This tutorial shows
why, and how to predict the actual speedup before spending a dollar on hardware.

::: {.callout-note}
## Prerequisites
Complete [Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline](00_hello_roofline.qmd). This tutorial assumes familiarity with
memory-bound vs. compute-bound regimes and the ridge point concept.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning Objectives

- **Calculate** the actual speedup between two GPUs for a given workload
- **Explain** why the binding constraint determines which spec matters
- **Predict** whether a hardware upgrade will help a specific model
- **Apply** the roofline model to hardware procurement decisions
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Background: The Two Specs That Matter

GPU vendors advertise peak FLOP/s prominently, yet every GPU also has a memory bandwidth
spec (in TB/s) that is equally important. Which spec determines actual performance
depends entirely on which **regime** the workload is in:

| Regime | Binding Constraint | Speedup Scales With |
|:-------|:-------------------|:--------------------|
| Memory-bound | HBM bandwidth (TB/s) | Bandwidth ratio between GPUs |
| Compute-bound | Peak arithmetic (FLOP/s) | FLOP/s ratio between GPUs |

The key numbers for this tutorial:

| Spec | A100 | H100 | Ratio |
|:-----|:-----|:-----|:------|
| Peak FP16 | `{python} f"{flops_a:.0f} TFLOP/s"` | `{python} f"{flops_h:.0f} TFLOP/s"` | **`{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`×** |
| HBM Bandwidth | `{python} f"{bw_a:.2f} TB/s"` | `{python} f"{bw_h:.2f} TB/s"` | **`{python} f"{bw_ratio:.1f}"`×** |

For a memory-bound workload, the speedup ceiling is `{python} f"{bw_ratio:.1f}"`×, regardless of the `{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`× compute improvement.
:::

## 1. Setup

```python
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine
```

---

## 2. Side-by-Side Hardware Comparison

Load both GPUs from the Silicon Zoo and confirm the specs:

```{python}
from mlsysim.show import table

a100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
h100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100

flops_a = a100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
flops_h = h100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
bw_a = a100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
bw_h = h100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude

table(
    ["Spec", "A100", "H100", "Ratio"],
    [
        ["Peak FP16 (TFLOP/s)", flops_a, flops_h, f"{flops_h/flops_a:.1f}x"],
        ["HBM BW (TB/s)", bw_a, bw_h, f"{bw_h/bw_a:.1f}x"],
        ["Ridge (FLOP/byte)", f"{ridge_a:.1f}", f"{ridge_h:.1f}", f"{ridge_h/ridge_a:.1f}x"]
    ]
)
```

The FLOP/s ratio is `{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`× (`{python} f"{flops_h:.0f}"` vs. `{python} f"{flops_a:.0f} TFLOP/s"`), whereas the bandwidth ratio is only `{python} f"{bw_ratio:.1f}"`× (`{python} f"{bw_h:.2f}"` vs. `{python} f"{bw_a:.2f} TB/s"`). The theoretical ridge point also
shifts from `{python} f"{ridge_a:.1f}"` to `{python} f"{ridge_h:.1f} FLOP/byte"`: the H100 has a *higher* ridge, meaning more workloads fall into the memory-bound
regime on the H100 than on the A100.

---

## 3. The Fallacy: LLM Inference Speedup

The "`{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`× speedup" claim can be tested with a workload that dominates production
today, Llama-3 8B inference at batch size 1:

```{python}
model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B

# Solve on both GPUs
prof_a100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=a100, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")
prof_h100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=h100, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")

lat_a = prof_a100.latency.to("ms").magnitude
lat_h = prof_h100.latency.to("ms").magnitude
speedup = lat_a / lat_h

table(
    ["", "A100", "H100", "Speedup"],
    [
        ["Bottleneck", prof_a100.bottleneck, prof_h100.bottleneck, ""],
        ["Latency", prof_a100.latency.to("ms"), prof_h100.latency.to("ms"), f"{speedup:.1f}x"],
        ["Throughput", prof_a100.throughput, prof_h100.throughput, ""]
    ]
)
```

Both GPUs report **memory-bound**. The actual speedup is approximately
**`{python} f"{speedup:.1f}"`×** (`{python} f"{lat_a:.2f} ms"` vs. `{python} f"{lat_h:.2f} ms"`), close to the `{python} f"{bw_ratio:.1f}"`× bandwidth ratio
rather than the `{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`× FLOP/s ratio. The remaining
`{python} f"{flops_ratio/speedup:.1f}"`× of the H100's compute advantage goes unused
for this workload.

**Sanity check:** Llama-3 8B at FP16 has `{python} f"{params_b:.2f}B"` parameters × 2 bytes = `{python} f"{weights_gb:.2f} GB"` of weights. On the A100
(`{python} f"{bw_a:.2f} TB/s"`), pure weight-streaming latency is `{python} f"{weights_gb:.2f} GB"` ÷ `{python} f"{bw_a:.2f} TB/s"` = **`{python} f"{min_lat_a:.1f} ms"`** (`{python} f"{lat_a:.1f} ms"` in `Engine.solve` after activation traffic and kernel launch tax). On the H100
(`{python} f"{bw_h:.2f} TB/s"`), pure weight-streaming latency is `{python} f"{weights_gb:.2f} GB"` ÷ `{python} f"{bw_h:.2f} TB/s"` = **`{python} f"{min_lat_h:.1f} ms"`** (`{python} f"{lat_h:.1f} ms"` in `Engine.solve`). The weight-streaming speedup is `{python} f"{min_lat_a:.1f}"` / `{python} f"{min_lat_h:.1f}"` = **`{python} f"{min_speedup:.2f}"`×**,
matching the bandwidth ratio, as expected for a memory-bound workload.

---

## 4. When `{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`× Matters: The Batch Size Crossover

The FLOP/s advantage takes effect only once the workload crosses into the compute-bound regime.
Sweeping batch size on both GPUs locates the crossover:

```{python}
rows = []
for batch in [1, 4, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]:
    pa = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=a100, batch_size=batch, precision="fp16")
    ph = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=h100, batch_size=batch, precision="fp16")

    la = pa.latency.to("ms").magnitude
    lh = ph.latency.to("ms").magnitude
    sp = la / lh if lh > 0 else 0
    ai = pa.arithmetic_intensity.to("flop/byte")

    rows.append([batch, f"{ai:~.1f}", pa.bottleneck, ph.bottleneck, f"{sp:.1f}x"])

table(["Batch Size", "Arithmetic Intensity", "A100 Bottleneck", "H100 Bottleneck", "Actual Speedup"], rows)
```

At batch size 256, where both GPUs are compute-bound, the speedup reaches `{python} f"{_sp_256:.1f}"`×, approaching the `{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`× compute ratio. The roofline plot below shows where Llama-3 8B at batch size 1 sits on the H100 relative to its `{python} f"{ridge_h:.1f} FLOP/byte"` ridge point:

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| warning: false
from mlsysim.viz.plots import plot_roofline

# Plot the H100 roofline and see where Llama-3 8B (batch 1) falls
fig, ax = plot_roofline(h100, workloads=[model])
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Insight

**The binding constraint determines which hardware spec matters.** For a memory-bound workload,
speedup scales with the bandwidth ratio (`{python} f"{bw_ratio:.1f}"`×). For a compute-bound workload, speedup scales
with the FLOP/s ratio (up to `{python} f"{flops_ratio:.1f}"`×). The transition happens at different batch sizes on each
GPU because the H100's higher ridge point (`{python} f"{ridge_h:.1f}"` vs. `{python} f"{ridge_a:.1f} FLOP/byte"`) means it *stays memory-bound longer*. In a
procurement decision, the first question is not "how many FLOP/s?" but "which regime
will the production workload operate in?"
:::

---

## 5. The Procurement Table: Three Generations

Extending the analysis across three GPU generations shows the trend:

```{python}
gpus = [
    ("V100", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.V100),
    ("A100", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100),
    ("H100", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100),
]

rows = []
for name, hw in gpus:
    p = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=hw, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")
    flops = hw.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
    bw = hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
    ridge = (hw.compute.peak_flops / hw.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude
    rows.append([name, flops, bw, f"{ridge:.1f}", p.latency.to("ms"), p.bottleneck])

table(["GPU", "TFLOP/s", "BW (TB/s)", "Ridge", "Latency", "Bottleneck"], rows)
```

Across three generations (from `{python} f"{flops_v:.0f} TFLOP/s"` and `{python} f"{bw_v:.1f} TB/s"` on the V100 to `{python} f"{flops_h:.0f} TFLOP/s"` and `{python} f"{bw_h:.2f} TB/s"` on the H100), compute has grown `{python} f"{flops_h/flops_v:.1f}"`× while bandwidth has grown `{python} f"{bw_h/bw_v:.1f}"`×. The theoretical ridge point rises from `{python} f"{ridge_v:.1f}"` to `{python} f"{ridge_a:.1f}"` to `{python} f"{ridge_h:.1f} FLOP/byte"`, which means **more workloads are memory-bound on newer hardware**. This is the
memory wall, and it is getting steeper with each generation.
